description:
ABOUT : Team Tiny Sparks, a multidisciplinary team of six school students united by one belief: Space Education Is for Everyone.

Combining research, technology, design, and storytelling, we created Adopt a Satellite—an interactive educational project that brings the stories of abandoned NASA space exploration hardware closer to young minds.

We believe that every space mission leaves behind more than hardware. It leaves behind discoveries, memories, and stories worth remembering.
summary:
Adopt a Satellite: Relic Map is an offline, single-file web app that tells the stories of 19 robotic spacecraft left on the Moon,on Mars,and in deep space, including Apollo 11, Viking 1, Spirit, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10, and Cassini. Each relic has a photo, a child-friendly story, a timeline, and NASA source links, so teachers can check every claim.

- Relic Map: 7 Moon, 8 Mars, and 4 deep-space records, each with an "Adopt this relic" button.
- Rescue / Remember: a re-entry game and a curator-style nameplate activity.
- Signal Lab: five Morse code levels, input by sound, flash, vibration, or telegraph key.
- Time Capsule: notes, a drawing canvas, voice notes stored on the device, PNG postcards, and backup export and import.
- Passport: badges and certificates for motivation.
- Bangla and English: one switch changes the whole app.
- Accessibility: keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels,reduced-motion support, and large touch targets. Vibration and flash offer non-sound ways to receive Morse signals.

Privacy and offline use: no accounts, no tracking, and no server. Progress stays on the device. Once saved, the app works without internet; only NASA source links need a connection.

Built in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript as one file of about 500 KB. Designed for low-connectivity schools in Bangladesh, especially hill and remote villages. It answers the challenge "Abandoned but not forgotten" by turning retired missions into stories children can understand, remember, and share.
details:
Adopt a Satellite: Relic Map is a privacy-first, offline space-education web app for children. It tells the stories of robotic spacecraft that humans left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. The whole app is one HTML file of about 500 KB. It needs no installation, server, account, or internet connection to run. Only the optional NASA source links need the internet.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Each abandoned machine is treated as a relic with a story. Learners open the Relic Map, choose one of nineteen records (seven on the Moon, eight on Mars, four in deep space), and read a child-friendly story, a timeline, coordinates where reliable, and NASA source links. The "Adopt this relic" button lets a child claim a relic as their own.

- Home: introduces the app and shows a "Relic of the day", chosen by date so every device shows the same relic.

- Rescue / Remember: a re-entry game, a curator-style nameplate activity, and a "My Opinion" box.

- Signal Lab: five Morse code levels, with input by sound, flash lamp, vibration, or telegraph key.

- Time Capsule: text notes, a drawing canvas, short voice notes stored on the device, PNG postcards, and backup export and import.

- Passport: badges and bronze, silver, and gold certificates, designed for motivation rather than testing.

A Bangla and English switch changes the whole interface and all story text.

BENEFITS

- Children read and write about space in their own language, Bangla or English.

- The file can be shared by USB drive, memory card, Bluetooth, or a school network, and then runs fully offline. Progress stays on the device.

- No accounts, tracking, analytics, advertising, or community features. Children enter only a nickname, which can be made up.

- Accessible by design: keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, reduced-motion support, dark mode, large touch targets, and Morse signals that can be felt through vibration or seen through a flash lamp.

- Each relic lists its NASA sources, so teachers can check every story.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want children in Bangladesh, especially in hill and remote villages, to learn about space through stories they can understand, remember, and share. The theme "Abandoned but not forgotten" becomes a learning activity: children choose to remember a machine's story rather than forget it. Next steps include a school pilot in a rural or hill area, read-aloud in Bangla and English, printable relic and Morse cards for schools without devices, and an Earth-Orbit Tracker for satellites around Earth (in development, not in the current file).

TESTING WITH CHILDREN

We tested the app with five children aged 6 to 12, with permission from their legal guardians. Each child tried part of the app: vibration-based Morse in Signal Lab, the Rescue / Remember activity, the Bangla and English switch with the Time Capsule, and the Relic Map with "Adopt this relic". Their comments showed that the vibration felt like a secret message they could decode, that the robot activity made them think about remembering a machine rather than bringing it back, that writing in Bangla made space feel closer, and that adopting a relic made them feel ownership. One child said they want to become a space engineer. This was an informal test, not a controlled study. It shows how these children felt. It does not measure learning outcomes.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- Code: plain HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript, with no framework. Web Audio API for Morse tones, Canvas 2D for drawing and postcards, Vibration API, MediaRecorder with IndexedDB for voice notes, and localStorage for progress.

- Images: WebP, embedded as base64, built with a Python 3 script (embed_images.py) and a browser tool (embed_tool.html).

- Testing: node --check for syntax, and a Playwright headless Chromium click-through.

- Hardware: any phone, tablet, or laptop with a modern browser. No special hardware is needed.

- Software and data: NASA NSSDCA, JPL Photojournal, NASA Science, LROC, and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal. ITU-R M.1677-1 for Morse timings. Licence: Apache 2.0.

- AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) for code suggestions and first drafts. ElevenLabs for the video voiceover. The team made all design, data, and storytelling decisions and checked the final work.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

We treat retired machines as relics that can be adopted. We teach Morse through touch and light as well as sound, and we build Bangla and English in from the start. We considered children's privacy first, then rural connectivity, accessibility for deaf and blind learners, the accuracy of NASA data, and whether children would enjoy the stories. Known limits are stated openly: five Mars records still show pending labels, and the Bangla text needs review by a native speaker.
